title: DNS failures, response codes, split horizon and DNSSEC
summary: NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL, REFUSED and timeout are different diagnoses. This lesson separates them, then covers the configurations that cause 'the record is right but the answer is wrong'.

sections.heading: Response codes and what they mean
sections.html:
RCODENameMeaningUsual cause
0NOERRORThe query succeededBut check the answer section: NOERROR with zero answers = NODATA
2SERVFAILThe resolver could not produce an answerUpstream failure, timeout to authoritative, DNSSEC validation failure, recursion disabled
3NXDOMAINThe name does not existTypo, deleted record, wrong zone, or the authoritative server genuinely has no such name
5REFUSEDThe server refuses to answer youACL: recursion denied, query from an unauthorised IP
1FORMERRMalformed queryBad EDNS handling, protocol mismatch
4NOTIMPQuery type not implementedRare

NODATA deserves its own line: NOERROR with an empty answer section means 'the name exists but has no record of that type'. Asking for an AAAA on an IPv4-only service returns NODATA, not NXDOMAIN. Confusing the two leads to wrong conclusions about whether a name exists.

sections.heading: Timeout is not an answer
sections.html:
A timeout means no response arrived, which is fundamentally different from a response saying 'no':

  • Timeout — path blocked, server down, firewall dropping UDP 53, or wrong nameserver address. The resolver eventually gives up; the application gets no answer at all. In practice glibc reports 'Temporary failure in name resolution', and dig shows no response.
  • SERVFAIL — a response arrived saying the resolver failed. Evidence that the network path works and the resolver is trying.
  • NXDOMAIN — a definitive, cacheable 'does not exist'.

This trio is the whole content of case study 11. The distinguishing command is just dig with timing: a timeout is slow (seconds) and produces no answer; SERVFAIL is fast and explicit.

sections.heading: Negative caching
sections.html:
NXDOMAIN and NODATA responses are cached, for the TTL in the SOA record's minimum field (RFC 2308). The practical failure: you create a record, but a resolver had already cached NXDOMAIN for that name and keeps returning it until the negative TTL expires.

Symptoms of negative caching rather than a bad record: the record checks out on the authoritative server (dig @ns1.example.com name works), but dig @1.1.1.1 name returns NXDOMAIN for a while. That is not 'propagation' — it is a cached negative answer ticking down.

sections.heading: Split-horizon DNS
sections.html:
Split horizon (split-brain) means the same name returns different answers depending on who asks: internal clients get a private address, external clients get a public one. Implemented with separate authoritative views, or with separate internal and external zones.

Failure modes are distinctive because they are client-dependent:

  • A client on the VPN gets a different answer than one on the office LAN.
  • An on-prem service resolves to a private range from outside, and connects fail — the record is not wrong, the view is.
  • Clients using a public resolver (1.1.1.1) see only the external view, so internal names either NXDOMAIN or resolve to a public IP that does not accept traffic.

Diagnosis: query the same name against different resolvers explicitly — dig @<internal-resolver> app.corp.example vs dig @1.1.1.1 app.corp.example. If they differ, you are looking at views, not at caching.

sections.heading: DNSSEC fundamentals
sections.html:
DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures so a resolver can verify that an answer came from the zone and was not altered in transit. It does not encrypt anything; that is DoT/DoH.

The chain: each zone signs its records (RRSIG), publishes a hash of its public key in its parent (DS), and the parent signs that delegation. Validation walks from the root's trust anchor downward. Key records: DNSKEY, DS, RRSIG, and NSEC/NSEC3 for authenticated denial of existence.

Practical consequences for a working engineer:

  • A DNSSEC chain break makes everything in the zone fail with SERVFAIL — including names that resolve fine when you query the authoritative server directly.
  • Expired RRSIGs cause outages on a schedule; monitoring signature expiry matters.
  • Resolvers differ in whether they validate; a validating resolver turns a broken chain into SERVFAIL instead of a wrong answer.

Because DNSSEC responses are large, they are also the classic victim of blocked UDP fragments or filtered DNS-over-TCP.

sections.heading: Common misconfigurations checklist
sections.html:
• Record exists only at the authoritative server, but the delegation (NS) points elsewhere.
  • Missing trailing dot: CNAME www.example.com. vs CNAME www.example.com (the latter becomes a relative name inside the zone).
  • Wrong RR type for the target: MX pointing at a CNAME; apex @ given a CNAME (breaks the whole zone including SOA/NS).
  • TTL 60 on everything, causing resolvers to hammer the authoritative server.
  • Reverse zone missing, so PTR lookups fail while forward works.
  • Search domain missing in DHCP (option 15/119), so short names fail but FQDNs work.
  • Internal names published only in an internal view, then queried from an external resolver.

checks.prompt: dig returns status: NXDOMAIN for a name you can see configured on the authoritative server. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A resolver has the earlier NXDOMAIN negatively cached, or you are hitting a different view/zone
checks.explanation: Negative caching or split-horizon views explain an NXDOMAIN for a record that exists authoritatively. Verify with dig @<authoritative> to bypass caches and views.

why_wrong.0: A dead server produces a timeout, not a clean NXDOMAIN.
why_wrong.3: Blocked UDP gives a timeout, not an authoritative-style NXDOMAIN.
why_wrong.1: TTL expiry causes a refetch, not non-existence.

It is cached like NXDOMAIN for the SOA minimum
It means the name does not exist

checks.explanation: SERVFAIL is a transient server-side failure signal. It is typically not cached (or cached very briefly), so retries can succeed where NXDOMAIN retries cannot.

why_wrong.1: Negative caching applies to NXDOMAIN/NODATA, not SERVFAIL.

checks.prompt: A domain intermittently fails to resolve. Explain how you would distinguish timeout, SERVFAIL and NXDOMAIN, and what each implies.

checklist.text: Timeout means no response arrived at all — path, firewall or server-down problem.
SERVFAIL means a response arrived but the resolver could not answer — upstream, DNSSEC or recursion issue.
NXDOMAIN is a definitive, cacheable 'does not exist' and implies a naming or view problem.
Use dig with explicit servers, and note elapsed time and status line.
Check both the configured resolver and the authoritative server to separate server truth from cache.

checks.reference: Run dig name repeatedly and read the status line plus timing. No response with multi-second waits is a timeout: suspect path filtering (UDP 53), a dead resolver, or a wrong nameserver address. A fast SERVFAIL means the resolver is reachable but cannot produce an answer: check upstream reachability, recursion ACLs and DNSSEC validation. A fast NXDOMAIN from the configured resolver but a correct answer from the authoritative server means negative caching or a split-horizon view. Intermittency points at multiple resolvers in resolv.conf with one broken, or at load-dependent packet loss.

connect.title: resolv.conf / systemd-resolved
connect.text: Multiple nameservers means failures can be intermittent depending on which is tried first.

connect.title: TLS / HTTP
connect.text: A DNSSEC-driven SERVFAIL looks like 'the site is down' to a user but is purely a naming failure.

connect.title: Case study 11
connect.text: The DNS timeout vs NXDOMAIN mission is built on this lesson.

interview.q: What is the difference between NXDOMAIN and SERVFAIL?
interview.a: NXDOMAIN is an authoritative 'this name does not exist' and is negatively cached. SERVFAIL means the resolver could not obtain a valid answer — upstream failure, timeout, or DNSSEC validation problem — and is usually not cached, so retrying can succeed.

interview.q: What is split-horizon DNS and how does it break things?
interview.a: The same name returns different answers depending on the source of the query, typically private addresses internally and public addresses externally. It breaks when a client uses the wrong view — for example a public resolver for an internal name — which looks like a wrong or missing record.
